sermon.title: Idolatry and Idols Part 1
sermon.speaker: Pastor David G. Kincer
sermon.summary: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer says America has its own idols in entertainment and compares them with the gods of ancient Corinth. He walks through 1 Corinthians 8, where Paul answers those who rely on human knowledge about food offered to idols, and explains the weak conscience and the stumbling block. He then connects idolatry to spiritual adultery and to 1 Corinthians 10, where Paul says to flee from idolatry and uses communion as an illustration.
sermon.transcript_source: This transcript comes from YouTube’s automatic English captions, which supply the timing and the words. Punctuation, capitalization and paragraphing were added by hand, and obvious caption errors were corrected; his wording was not rewritten. “[unclear]” marks a word or name that was not clear. Editor note: caption errors for some names were corrected where the meaning was clear (“Poseidon,” “Sceva,” “Kardashians,” “smorgasbord”); the words around “this [unclear] fella” and two other spots are marked [unclear]. He names several entertainers and makes claims about them; they appear only in the transcript and are his words, not verified by this site. The Scripture shown is NKJV; where he reads Scripture aloud he often uses King James wording.

chunks.section_question: Do we have idols in America today?
chunks.short_answer: He says in America “we do not have a tradition or custom to really worship” carved images, “but we do have our own idols.” He points to American Idol, where someone is made into a musical idol whom teenagers “adore,” and says music and TV develop the minds of most young people, who “imitate their idol.”
chunks.text:
Today in America, we do not have a tradition or custom to really worship and--and uh--follow idols, images created into gods. But we do have our own idols. American Idol is called American Idol. Why? Because they’re trying to make someone into a musical idol where the teenagers especially will adore them, wear the clothes that they wear, wear the hairstyle that they wear, and embrace the message that they’re trying to get across. These three judges, Steve Tyler, claims to be a Catholic, but he lives with women, and he aborted a five-month-old son and all kinds of other debauchery, drugs, sex, and everything else.

You think he cares about the moral condition of these people coming to be the next American Idol? No, he doesn’t care about the moral condition. He can call himself a Catholic all he wants. The Bible says, “You know them by their fruits.” Jennifer Lopez. She was raised in a Catholic home. She was a Buddhist a few years ago and now she switched over to Scientology. She’s just, you know, smorgasbord. She has no problem playing nude scenes in movies and uh all kinds of other uh immoral things. Randy Jackson is from a Catholic family, but on the show he wears voodoo beads. He is from Louisiana and voodoo is big down there. Are you there? You think these judges care about whether these people wind up good or not?

Or what they told him about this [unclear] fella, this young teenage rapper. They said, “Boy, you you you you win and you’re going to get all the girls you want.” This is what the judges told this young teenager. See, the focus is on sex, pleasure, partying, drinking, just a loose life. See, it’s idolatry. And they got the show pegged right. American Idol. Now, that’s not the only reality show. There’s other ones. The Kardashians is one, and I’ve never seen it, but wouldn’t want to see it, but I read about in the newspapers all the time, and other things. You see, we don’t have idols. We have living people that are idols. We have entertainment that we idolize. You know what develops the minds of most young people in America today?

Music. You know what the second development of minds of most young people today? TV. The media. Absolutely. And that’s why kids dress like they dress, wear their hair like they do, and so forth. They imitate their idol. So idolatry in America is very prevalent, but we don’t have these images and stuff like Corinth had. Here is just a few of their idols, their gods. Okay. Now, all of these idols were served with sacrifices, whether plants or meat, incense, music, prayers. They were common to all.

chunks.short_answer: He says “the conclusion of this approach to idols is not to partake of idols nor food sacrificed to idols.” In chapter 10 Paul “switches abruptly back to idolatry” with “flee from idolatry.” He says Israel in the wilderness shows that “just because you have the presence of God and you read the Bible does not mean you are pleasing to God.”
chunks.text:
The conclusion of this approach to idols is not to partake of idols nor food sacrificed to idols. That’s his conclusion, isn’t it? And he approached it from the human intellectual standpoint. Now, as Paul’s style is, he’s going to give another approach to the idol question. The next chapter deals with ministry. He’s establishing himself as ministry. The next chapter deals with Israel in the wilderness proving that just because you have the presence of God and you read the Bible does not mean you are pleasing to God.

And in chapter 10 he switches abruptly back to idolatry. Chapter 10 verse 14. Wherefore, when you see wherefore, you got to take note what it’s there for. For this reason, flee from idolatry. What’s he saying? What’s he saying directly now? Flee from idolatry. Okay. For what reason? He’s going to give it to us. First, he’s going to butter us up and tell us, I speak to wise men. Judge you what I say. You guys are a bunch of intelligent people. You can judge this. Here he is telling us to judge what he’s saying. And what’s America big on? Judge not, let you be not judged.

faqs.question: What does he say American Idol shows about idolatry?
faqs.answer: He says the show tries to “make someone into a musical idol where the teenagers especially will adore them.” He says “the focus is on sex, pleasure, partying, drinking, just a loose life. See, it’s idolatry.”

faqs.question: What does he say shapes the minds of young people the most?
faqs.answer: He says music is first and TV, “the media,” is second, and “that’s why kids dress like they dress, wear their hair like they do.”

faqs.question: What did the Romans and Greeks believe about the afterlife?
faqs.answer: He says for the Romans, if you were good, “you went to the Milky Way,” and for the Greeks, “you went to Hades.”

faqs.question: What was the Pantheon?
faqs.answer: He says it was “where you could go and any God you wanted to worship was there,” so you did not have to go to a specific temple.

faqs.question: Why does Paul begin by talking about knowledge?
faqs.answer: He says some in the Corinthian church “had it all figured out through human knowledge just like today,” so Paul tackles that first, and notes that “knowledge puffs up. It makes us proud.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: Now concerning things offered to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love edifies.

faqs.question: How does Paul deal with human thinking about spiritual problems?
faqs.answer: He says Paul “knows his Bible,” and “he’s going to neutralize this human thinking factor in trying to find solutions to spiritual problems,” citing what the Bible already says about not being wise in your own eyes.

scriptures.text_nkjv: Be of the same mind toward one another. Do not set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Do not be wise in your own opinion.

faqs.question: What does he say godliness is?
faqs.answer: He says godliness is pleasing God, not pleasing your friend or your spouse. He says “living to please God is the final measuring stick of anything you believe.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: If anyone teaches otherwise and does not consent to wholesome words, even the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which accords with godliness,

faqs.question: Does he say there is more than one way to God?
faqs.answer: No. He says “there is no other gods” and “there isn’t any other way to God but God’s way.”

faqs.question: Does what you eat make you more spiritual?
faqs.answer: He says food “has nothing to do with spirituality,” including diet and healthy eating, and that if you honor your parents and obey God’s word, he says the Bible promises long life and health.

faqs.question: What does Romans 14 say about eating?
faqs.answer: He reads that one believes he may eat all things while another who is weak eats herbs, and that the one who eats should not despise the one who does not, and “let not him which eats not judge him that eats.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: Receive one who is weak in the faith, but not to disputes over doubtful things. For one believes he may eat all things, but he who is weak eats only vegetables. Let not him who eats despise him who does not eat, and let not him who does not eat judge him who eats; for God has received him.

faqs.question: What is a stumbling block in 1 Corinthians 8?
faqs.answer: He says Paul is appealing not to their mental understanding but to their conscience, “that what you do can hurt other people,” and that your liberty can become a stumbling block to those who are weak.

scriptures.text_nkjv: But beware lest somehow this liberty of yours become a stumbling block to those who are weak.

faqs.question: Why does Paul call some believers weak?
faqs.answer: He asks, “why do you think he’s calling them weak?” and answers that it is to make them “feel more important. We love it. We like to be the one that’s better. But wait till he gets done with it.”

faqs.question: What does he say most Christians do when they read the Bible?
faqs.answer: He says “they read passages in the Bible and they come up with human thinking instead of the mind of the spirit.”

faqs.question: What does he conclude about people being offended?
faqs.answer: He says he finally decided “I’m just going to do what I know is right. And if they get offended, that’s their problem. And that was a big freedom.”

faqs.question: Does he say Christians should never judge?
faqs.answer: He says Paul tells them to judge what he is saying: “Here he is telling us to judge what he’s saying.” He contrasts that with “Judge not, let you be not judged,” and says the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

scriptures.text_nkjv: “Judge not, that you be not judged.
